title: Ten Million Riders in the Queue for ofo's Bike Deposits
dek: In December 2018 ofo's founder told staff he had weighed bankruptcy many times, chose to keep going, and left millions of riders waiting for their deposits.

story.event: Choosing to carry on, not file for bankruptcy, as more than ten million riders waited for deposit refunds
story.summary: In December 2018 ofo, the Beijing bike-sharing company Dai Wei had started at Peking University, had gone months without new funding while more than ten million users queued online for refunds of 99- or 199-yuan deposits and a court restricted his spending. In a letter to staff on 19 December Dai said he had often considered bankruptcy but would keep going and try to meet the company's duties to users. Refunds came slowly; in 2021 at least 15 million people were reported still waiting.
paragraphs: On Monday 17 December 2018, more than a hundred people stood in the lobby of ofo's headquarters in Zhongguancun, Beijing, and in the street outside, let in a batch at a time. Each wanted back a deposit of 99 or 199 yuan, roughly $14 to $29, paid to unlock the company's yellow bicycles. Caixin reported that visitors wrote down their details, including bank account numbers, and were told they would be paid within days; ofo said walk-in claims would join the online queue in order.

The company had begun at Peking University, where Dai Wei and fellow members of the university's cycling association turned a struggling cycling-tour business into a campus bike-sharing scheme; by October 2015 it had more than 2,000 bikes and 20,000 users. By 2017 ofo said it ran more than 10 million bikes in 250 cities across 20 countries. It raised $700 million in July 2017 and more than $850 million in March 2018. Then, Caixin reported, nine months passed without new money, refund requests climbed from September, and suppliers sued over unpaid bills. A Beijing court order dated 4 December restricted Dai's personal spending.

On Wednesday 19 December Dai wrote to his staff. He said he had thought countless times of dissolving the company and filing for bankruptcy, and that ofo had misjudged how its outside environment was changing from late 2017. More than 10 million users were by then waiting online for refunds, about 1.1 billion yuan even at the lower deposit. He chose to carry on: every yuan would have to cover three needs, refunds, suppliers and operations, and he pledged to try hard to meet the company's responsibilities to users. Two days later the Ministry of Transport urged ofo to open more refund channels and speed them up.

The money came back slowly. In July 2019 an ofo employee told reporters that about 10,000 refunds were paid each day; Asia Times, watching the queue move, put the figure nearer 3,500, against some 16 million applications. In 2020 the bike app became a shopping site offering store credit instead of cash. In November 2021 Sixth Tone reported that at least 15 million people were still waiting, and that Dai had left the company during the 2018 crisis.

quote.text: Is it not reason that my conscience should be much more engaged when men simply rely upon it?  In a bond, my faith owes nothing, because it has nothing lent it
quote.translator: Charles Cotton (1685), ed. W. C. Hazlitt
quote.source_title: Essays of Michel de Montaigne — Complete, tr. Charles Cotton, Project Gutenberg eBook #3600
quote.connection: Montaigne felt more bound by what people left on trust than by anything a court could enforce. ofo's suppliers had lawsuits and the state had court orders; the ten million riders had only the company's word that their 99 or 199 yuan would come back.

reflection: It is easy to read this as a story about billions, but much of what ofo owed came in small sums from people who never thought to ask for a contract. Small trusts are the ones most easily left at the back of the queue, because nobody sues over them.

You hold some of these too: a promise to look at a colleague's work, a word to your family about when you will be home, a reply you said you would send. None is large, and each was given on trust. When one cannot be kept, telling the person plainly, and soon, is still a way of honouring it.
invitation: Think of one small promise you made this week that is slipping. Before midday, either keep it or tell the person honestly when you now can.

sources.title: Ofo Founder Blacklisted by Court Amid Debt Woes

sources.title: Ofo on verge of bankruptcy
sources.supports: Dai's letter: he had thought countless times of dissolving the company and applying for bankruptcy, and the firm must turn every renminbi into three; more than 10 million refund requests (citing TechNode); more than 100 people queuing and being asked for banking details.

sources.title: Bike-sharing company ofo hit with spending restriction order amid bankruptcy fears
sources.supports: Court order of 4 December restricting Dai's and ofo's spending; Dai's letter saying he had repeatedly considered dissolving the company and filing for bankruptcy, that every yuan must be turned into three, and that ofo failed to correctly assess the changing external environment from the end of the previous year; online refund queue over 10 million; deposits of 99 to 199 yuan; March 2018 round of $866 million.

sources.title: Ministry of Transport urges ofo to expedite online refund process
sources.supports: Ministry of Transport statement of Friday 21 December urging ofo to add refund channels, cut costs and expedite refunds; at least 11 million online refund applicants; about 1.1 billion yuan at 99 yuan a deposit; Dai's pledge in his Wednesday letter to try hard to meet responsibilities to users.

sources.title: Ministry tells Ofo to return deposits
sources.supports: Ministry of Transport urging ofo to return deposits and speed up refunds; more than 10 million online refund applications as of 20 December; consumption restrictions on Dai after unpaid debts to logistics companies, bike makers and other suppliers.

research_notes: Queue size disagrees across December 2018 reports: 'more than 10 million' (Caixin, China Daily, CGTN 20 December, The China Project citing TechNode), 'nearly 11 million' (AFP) and 'at least 11 million' (CGTN 21 December); SCMP's 'nearly 12 million' could not be used (blocked). The story uses the conservative 'more than 10 million'. The 1.1 billion yuan figure is CGTN's arithmetic at the lower 99-yuan deposit, and is stated as such. Later figures: Asia Times (July 2019) gives 16 million applications and contrasts an anonymous ofo employee's 10,000 refunds a day with its reporter's estimate of about 3,500; Sixth Tone (November 2021) says at least 15 million were still waiting. Both are attributed. March 2018 funding is 'more than $850 million' (AFP) and $866 million (CGTN); the story uses AFP's wording. Court order: Caixin and CGTN date it 4 December; China Daily says restrictions were imposed on 20 December, which is when they were reported; the story says 'dated 4 December'. Founders: PKU News names three (Zhang Siding, Dai Wei, Xue Dong) and Beijing Review says Dai and two others from the cycling association, while other accounts give five; the story says 'fellow members' without a number. Campus launch: Beijing Review says 2014, PKU News says bikes were bought from May 2015; the story gives the October 2015 numbers only. Dai's letter is known only through translations (renminbi vs yuan; 'misjudgement' vs 'failed to correctly assess'), so it is paraphrased rather than quoted. Causes of the collapse are limited to Dai's own admission of misjudgement; the story attributes no other blame. arc is set to hard-responsibility rather than the slate's closure: Dai's decision was not to close, and ofo was never formally wound up in these sources (Sixth Tone says it still existed in 2021). 'ofo (Dongxia Datong)' uses the operating company named by Caixin. Montaigne's passage contrasts obligations of trust with contractual bonds; it is applied by analogy to deposits.
